# TASK: Group penguins into three body-mass categories and compare their average flipper length

Load the packages:
```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
library(tidyverse)
```

Your goal:

Create a new column, `mass_category`, in the `penguins` dataset that categorizes each penguin by its body mass (variable `body_mass_g`). If `body_mass_g` is:

* greater than 5000, label it "Large"
* between 4000 and 5000 (inclusive), label it "Medium"
* less than 4000, label it "Small"

Then use `group_by()` to group the data by `mass_category`, and use `summarize()` to calculate the average flipper length (variable `flipper_length_mm`) for each category.


## Answer using a function we already know: `case_when()`

Use the `dplyr` functions `mutate()` and `case_when()` to create the new `mass_category` variable. Once you are done, revise your code to add a condition that checks for missing values in `body_mass_g` and sets them to `NA_character_` in `mass_category`.

Solution without checking for NA:
```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    mass_category = case_when(
      body_mass_g > 5000 ~ "Large",
      body_mass_g >= 4000 & body_mass_g <= 5000 ~ "Medium",
      body_mass_g < 4000 ~ "Small"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(mass_category) |>
  summarize(
    avg_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Solution checking for NA:
```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(
    mass_category = case_when(
      is.na(body_mass_g) ~ NA_character_,
      body_mass_g > 5000 ~ "Large",
      body_mass_g >= 4000 & body_mass_g <= 5000 ~ "Medium",
      body_mass_g < 4000 ~ "Small"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(mass_category) |>
  summarize(
    avg_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Both versions give the same output: when `body_mass_g` is missing, none of the conditions is TRUE, so `case_when()` returns NA. Adding the NA check is still good practice, because it makes the handling of missing data explicit and easy to see.

Tip: `case_when()` checks the conditions in order and stops at the first one that is TRUE. Once penguins above 5000 have been labeled "Large", the condition `body_mass_g >= 4000` alone would be enough to identify "Medium".


## Answer using a new concept from today: the `ifelse()` function

Remember the syntax from the slides:
```
ifelse(condition to be evaluated,
       action performed when condition is TRUE,
       action performed when condition is FALSE)
```

Solution without checking for NA:
```{r}
# start by labeling every penguin "Small", 
# then overwrite the label only where each condition is TRUE

penguins |>
  mutate(mass_category = "Small") |>
  mutate(mass_category = ifelse(body_mass_g >= 4000 & body_mass_g <= 5000, 
                                "Medium",
                                mass_category)) |>
  mutate(mass_category = ifelse(body_mass_g > 5000, 
                                "Large",
                                mass_category)) |>
  group_by(mass_category) |>
  summarize(avg_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Notice that the penguins with missing `body_mass_g` already end up as NA here. This is because `ifelse()` returns NA whenever its condition is NA. The explicit NA check below gives the same result, but it makes your intention clear.

Solution checking for NA:
```{r}
# start with NA for missing values and "Small" for everyone else, 
# then overwrite the label only where each condition is TRUE

penguins |>
  mutate(mass_category = ifelse(is.na(body_mass_g), 
                                NA_character_, 
                                "Small")) |>
  mutate(mass_category = ifelse(body_mass_g >= 4000 & body_mass_g <= 5000, 
                                "Medium", 
                                mass_category)) |>
  mutate(mass_category = ifelse(body_mass_g > 5000, 
                                "Large", 
                                mass_category)) |>
  group_by(mass_category) |>
  summarize(avg_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Solution with nested `ifelse()` (works and correct, not recommended until you have good command of this function):
```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(mass_category = ifelse(body_mass_g > 5000, "Large",
                                ifelse(body_mass_g >= 4000, "Medium", "Small"))) |>
  group_by(mass_category) |>
  summarize(avg_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

This version works and gives the same result: the second `ifelse()` is only reached when `body_mass_g > 5000` is FALSE, so `body_mass_g >= 4000` is enough to identify "Medium". However, nested `ifelse()` statements quickly become hard to read and easy to get wrong, especially with more categories. When you have more than two categories, `case_when()` is the clearer choice.


## Answer using a new concept from today: a set of `if`/`else` statements

In this case, you need to use `rowwise()` at the top of your code so that your `if` and `else` statements are applied to each row of the data frame. In practice, `rowwise()` forces R to process each row individually (i.e., it treats each row as its own group). The structure looks like this:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
penguins |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    # add your if and else statements here
  )
```

Solution (must include the check for NA at the top):
```{r}
penguins |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    mass_category = if (is.na(body_mass_g)) {
      NA_character_
    } else if (body_mass_g > 5000) {
      "Large"
    } else if (body_mass_g >= 4000 && body_mass_g <= 5000) {
      "Medium"
    } else {
      "Small"
    }
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(mass_category) |>
  summarize(
    avg_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Why must the NA check come first? Unlike `ifelse()`, `if` cannot handle NA: `if (NA)` stops with the error "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed". Checking for NA first makes sure the other conditions are only tested on penguins that have a body mass.

Note that inside `if()` we use `&&` instead of `&`. Both work here, but `&&` is the standard choice for `if()`, because `if()` always tests a single TRUE/FALSE value.


## KEY DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THESE APPROACHES

* `case_when()` and `ifelse()` are **vectorized**: they evaluate a condition across all elements (rows) of an entire column (i.e., a vector) at the same time.

* `if`/`else` statements are **not vectorized**: they evaluate a condition one element at a time. To apply them to a data frame, you need a `for` loop or another approach (such as `rowwise()`, as we did here) to evaluate each element (row) individually.


## TAKE HOME

1. `case_when()` and `ifelse()` have similar uses: manipulating variables (recoding, categorizing, etc.) based on conditions. Use them inside data frames and with the tidyverse. They are also much faster than `rowwise()` on large datasets.

2. Use `if`/`else` outside data frames, for so-called "flow control" (i.e., deciding which code runs based on a condition). Today's slides include examples of standard uses of `if`/`else` statements.
